quickAnswer: Termessos and Sagalassos are Pisidia's two most dramatic mountain cities, sitting at 1,050 and 1,500–1,700 metres respectively. Termessos requires a steep, rocky 30-minute uphill hike from the car park inside Güllük Dağı National Park, while Sagalassos lies two hours north of Antalya and stays reliably snow-free from May through October.

body.text: Coastal ruins near Antalya are flat, hot, and crowded with tour coaches. Climb into the Taurus Mountains behind the city and the mood shifts completely. This termessos sagalassos guide covers the practical realities of visiting two high-altitude Pisidian strongholds—one wild and largely unexcavated, the other a masterwork of archaeological restoration.
How steep is the hike into Termessos National Park?

The climb from the upper car park at Termessos to the gymnasium, agora, and cliffside theatre is genuinely steep, gaining roughly 150 vertical metres over 900 metres of loose limestone scree and uneven ancient paving. Expect 25 to 35 minutes of steady uphill walking each way, plus another 90 minutes scrambling among the ruins.

Sitting at 1,050 metres inside [Güllük Dağı-Termessos National Park](https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/1412/) on UNESCO's Tentative List, Termessos is famous for turning back Alexander the Great in 333 BC—he judged the mountain pass too costly to storm and marched north instead. The park sits 32 kilometres northwest of Antalya (about 45 minutes by car), followed by a winding 9-kilometre paved climb from the park gate to the car park.

There is no shuttle bus from the car park to the ruins, no café inside the archaeological zone, and minimal signage. Anyone with knee issues or limited mobility will struggle on the descent over loose gravel. For fit hikers, however, standing alone in the 4,200-seat theatre above sheer 600-metre canyon walls beats almost any coastal site in Türkiye.
Why is Sagalassos's Antonine Fountain worth the 2-hour drive?

Built between 161 and 180 AD during Marcus Aurelius's reign, Sagalassos's 28-metre-wide Antonine Fountain still pours cold Taurus mountain spring water down its restored marble facade—the only Roman monumental nymphaeum in Anatolia running from its original ancient water source. Combined with the 9,000-seat theatre at 1,600 metres, it justifies the two-hour drive north of Antalya.

Located above the town of Ağlasun in Burdur Province, [Sagalassos Archaeological Site](https://muze.gov.tr/muze-detay?sectionId=SAG01&distId=MRK) sits between 1,450 and 1,700 metres and has been on the [UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List](https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5409/) since 2009. Excavated since 1990, the city was buried by erosion after 7th-century earthquakes and spared heavy looting.

The [Antonine Nymphaeum](https://www.turkishmuseums.com/blog/detail/4-must-see-artifacts-in-sagalassos/10056/4) was reassembled using seven distinct coloured stones and original architectural blocks, completed in 2010. Active restoration continues nearby: teams from [Burdur Mehmet Akif Ersoy University](https://mehmetakif.edu.tr/en/content/12253/1/sagalassosta-1800-year-old-hadrianus-fountain-is-coming-to-light) have been reconstructing the two-storey Hadrian's Fountain just down the colonnaded street.

body.text: What shoes and water are required?

Both sites demand proper closed-toe trail shoes or light hiking boots with lugged rubber soles—leave flat sneakers, leather sandals, and flip-flops at the hotel. Carry at least 1.5 litres of water per person at Termessos and 1 litre at Sagalassos, as there are no water stations once you pass the ticket gates.
Mountain ruins punish casual packing. Use this quick kit checklist before leaving Antalya:

items: Footwear: Ankle-supporting trail runners or hiking boots for loose karst limestone at Termessos and steep terraced steps at Sagalassos.
Hydration & snacks: Buy water in Antalya or Ağlasun; Termessos has only basic restrooms near the car park and zero vendors on the trail.
Sun & wind layers: UV exposure is sharper above 1,500 metres, and mountain ridges turn breezy even when Antalya's coast sits at 30°C.
Offline maps: Mobile reception drops in Termessos's pine ravines; download offline trail pins before leaving the car.

body.text: Which months are free of snow at Sagalassos?

Sagalassos is reliably free of snow and ice from May through October, with late May, June, September, and early October delivering the clearest mountain visibility and comfortable daytime temperatures (18–26°C). Snow regularly blankets the Upper Agora between late November and March, and April can still bring muddy trails or late sleet.

Because Sagalassos sits nearly a mile above sea level, its climate bears little resemblance to Antalya's coastline. On a mild 20°C coastal day in March, Sagalassos can be 4°C with icy wind and frozen puddles across the agora paving. Termessos, 500 metres lower, rarely holds deep snow and stays hikeable from March through November, though winter rain makes its limestone trails treacherous.

Can you combine both in one day? Technically yes, if you leave Antalya at 07:30 with a private driver, hike Termessos for two hours, and reach Sagalassos by early afternoon. In practice, we advise splitting them or pairing Sagalassos with an overnight stay in Ağlasun so neither site feels rushed. If you prefer flatter coastal Roman sites first, see our [Aspendos, Perge and Side guide](https://itineraryofturkiye.com/blog/aspendos-perge-side).

faq.q: Can you visit Termessos and Sagalassos on the same day from Antalya?
faq.a: It is possible only with a private car and an 07:30 start: spend 2.5 hours at Termessos, drive 1 hour 40 minutes north to Sagalassos via the D650 highway, and return to Antalya by 18:30. Most travellers enjoy them far more on separate days.

faq.q: Is Sagalassos open in winter if it snows?
faq.a: Yes, Sagalassos generally remains open year-round under Turkish Ministry of Culture winter hours (typically 08:30–17:00), unless heavy snowfall blocks the final 7-kilometre mountain access road from Ağlasun. Always check road conditions locally in winter.

faq.q: Are there guided tours to Termessos and Sagalassos?
faq.a: Standard group bus tours rarely visit either site because coaches cannot easily navigate the steep approach roads and group pacing clashes with the hiking required. Hiring a private licensed guide and driver is the most practical way to visit.

faq.q: Is the water from the Antonine Fountain at Sagalassos safe to drink?
faq.a: No. While the fountain is fed by natural mountain spring water, visitors are strictly prohibited from climbing into the basin, touching the marble stonework, or drinking from the monument. Bring your own bottled water.

faq.q: Where are the original statues from Sagalassos displayed?
faq.a: The marble originals—including the colossal statues of Emperor Marcus Aurelius and Hadrian—are housed in the Burdur Archaeological Museum, roughly 40 minutes west of Sagalassos. Replicas stand inside the niches of the Antonine Fountain on site.

faq.q: Are children allowed on the Termessos hike?
faq.a: Yes, active children aged seven and older usually enjoy scrambling around Termessos, provided they wear grippy shoes and stay supervised near the unfenced theatre drops and ancient cistern openings. Strollers are completely unusable on the trail.
